title: Chapter 116 — Onboarding and The 90-Day Ramp
intro: The first week, the curriculum as ramp plan, gates and ramp economics.

sections.title: The First Week Sets the Tone
sections.content:
A new hire's first week determines whether they feel invested in or thrown to the wolves. Structure the first week around learning — the showroom, the products, the team, the tools, and the culture.

Do not put them on the floor to sell on day one. They are not ready. And a bad first customer interaction can damage their confidence before it has a chance to develop.

Shadowing, observation, product training, and CRM orientation come first. Selling comes when they have the foundation.

sections.title: The 90-Day Gate System
sections.content:
Break the ramp into three phases with clear expectations at each gate.

Day 30: can they walk the floor, explain product categories, and follow the first five steps of the 10 Steps?
Day 60: can they run the full 10 Steps independently with coaching support nearby?
Day 90: can they manage the complete process — greeting through follow-up — on their own?

Gates are not pass/fail tests. They are checkpoints that tell you whether the person is on track and what they need more help with.

sections.title: Ramp Economics
sections.content:
New hires cost money before they make money. That is the investment. The question is whether the investment produces a return.

A structured ramp reduces the time to productivity. An unstructured ramp — throwing someone on the floor and hoping for the best — extends it. Every extra week of ramp time costs money in lost sales and management time.

The store that onboards well retains better and produces faster. The store that onboards poorly burns through hires and wonders why nobody sticks.

sections.title: Coaching Rule
sections.content:
When evaluating onboarding, ask:

Is the first week structured — or chaotic?
Are there clear gates at 30, 60, and 90 days?
Is the new hire shadowing top performers — or figuring it out alone?
Is the ramp producing independent salespeople — or dependent ones?
